title: Headlines from the New York Times
text:
Have you ever been curious about the hidden patterns behind New York Times headlines (…especifically Bill Clinton and Bosnia)? If so, you’re in for a treat! Using the RTextTools package, we’ll explore a dataset of over 3,000 headlines to show trends in the news of 1996 to 2006.
The dataset I am using comes from the RTextTools package and is documented
here. It is a dataset with labeled headlines from The New York Times, compiled by Professor Amber E. Boydstun at the University of California, Davis. As I stated previously, it contains information from 1996 to 2001.
It contains five variables — Article_ID, Date, Title, Subject, and Topic.Code.

library(tidyverse)
library(RTextTools)
data("NYTimes", package = "RTextTools")
nyt <- as_tibble(NYTimes)
head(nyt)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  Article_ID Date     Title                                   Subject Topic.Code
       <int> <fct>    <fct>                                   <fct>        <int>
1      41246 1-Jan-96 Nation's Smaller Jails Struggle To Cop… Jails …         12
2      41257 2-Jan-96 FEDERAL IMPASSE SADDLING STATES WITH I… Federa…         20
3      41268 3-Jan-96 Long, Costly Prelude Does Little To Al… Conten…         20
4      41279 4-Jan-96 Top Leader of the Bosnian Serbs Now Un… Bosnia…         19
5      41290 5-Jan-96 BATTLE OVER THE BUDGET: THE OVERVIEW; … Battle…          1
6      41302 7-Jan-96 South African Democracy Stumbles on Ol… politi…         19


Clinton was all over the news in the late 1990s. Here is a vizualisation of such:

nyt_clinton_week <- nyt |>
  mutate(
    title_lower = str_to_lower(Title),
    has_clinton = str_detect(title_lower, "\\bclinton\\b"),
    date = dmy(Date),
    week = lubridate::floor_date(date, "week")
  ) |>
  filter(has_clinton, !is.na(week)) |>
  group_by(week) |>
  summarise(n = n())

ggplot(nyt_clinton_week, aes(x = week, y = n)) +
  geom_line(color = "blue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "blue") +
  labs(
    title = "Fig 1: NYT headlines mentioning `Clinton`, grouped by week (1996-2006)",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Number of Headlines"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8)








The story in figure 1 is clear! Clinton was seeking presidential re-election in 1996, then back in office in 1997 and then, from 1998 to 2000, the Lewinsky scandal and impeachment took place. In the 2000s, he was no longer in office, explaining the lack of mentions about him.
In 1997, Clinton visited Bosnia (did you know?). In that topic, how often is Bosnia mentioned in this time frame in the New York Times Headlines? Given Bosnia’s situation gained particular international attention in the very late 90s, let’s analyse the data in this dataset going till 1999.

library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(RTextTools)

nyt_balkan <- as_tibble(NYTimes) |>
  mutate(
    title_lower   = str_to_lower(Title),
    subject_lower = str_to_lower(Subject),
    date  = dmy(Date),
    week  = floor_date(date, "week", week_start = 1),
    has_bosnia = str_detect(title_lower,
      "\\bbosnian?\\b|\\bbosnia-?herzegovina\\b|\\bsarajevo\\b|\\bbalkans?\\b"
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(week))

count_bosnia_by_week <- nyt_balkan |>
  filter(has_bosnia) |>
  count(week, name = "n")

ggplot(count_bosnia_by_week, aes(x = week, y = n)) +
  geom_line(color = "black") +
  geom_point(color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Fig 2: NYT headlines mentioning Bosnia-related terms (weekly, 1996–1999)",
    x = "Week", y = "Number of Headlines"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)







lookaround <- nyt_balkan |>
  mutate(before_in = str_extract(title_lower, "(?<=\\bin\\s)\\w+")) |>
  filter(before_in == "bosnia") |>
  count(Subject)

ggplot(lookaround, aes(y = Subject, x = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "Fig 3: Subjects appearing with 'in Bosnia'",
    subtitle = "1996-1999",
    x = "Subject", y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








The mentions of Bosnia in the NYT headlines in figure 2 reflect its situation in the late 90s. This idea is further further complemented by figure 3. Mentions spike in early 1996 as post-Dayton peacekeeping and reconstruction in Bosnia dominated coverage, then fade through 1997–98. They surge again in 1999 when Balkans-wide news (especially the Kosovo conflict) drives headlines.

title: A Room with an Ocean View
text:
Let’s imagine the following scenario: in a beautiful sea-side university, there are 500 students total and 200 rooms with a beautiful view to the sea. If you are like me, you would want to have a room with a view to the sea as well. For the purpose of this simulation, let’s assume everyone wants to have a room with a view to the sea.
Because everyone wants to have a room view a view, the university has decided to allocate these special rooms through a lottery system. Students are given a random lottery number that determines the order in which they can pick their room. The earlier your number, the better your chances of getting a sea-view room.
In this simulation, I’ll model the housing lottery by randomly assigning both the order in which students pick and the rooms available. I’ll then repeat the process 200 times to estimate how likely each lottery position is to end up with a room that has a sea view. IN other words, I’ll use one function to simulate a full housing draw and a mapping function to repeat the simulation across all positions, allowing me to estimate the probability of getting a sea-view room for each possible lottery number.

set.seed(47) # I chose 47 as the seed because of Pomona College.
library(tidyverse)

# this function runs one random housing draw 
housing_lottery <- function(total_students = 500, view_rooms = 200){
  order <- sample.int(total_students) # random lottery order
  tibble(
    order_number = 1:total_students,
    room_type = if_else(order <= view_rooms, "beautiful_view", "regular")
  )
}

#  this function will help me find how often a position gets a view room
#  (it now uses a lightweight simulation to speed things up dramatically)
position_success <- function(order_spot, trials = 200,
                             total_students = 500, view_rooms = 200){
  mean(
    replicate(trials, {
      order <- sample.int(total_students)  # random lottery order
      pick_rank <- match(order_spot, order)
      pick_rank <= view_rooms
    })
  )
}

spots <- 1:500
chance_by_spot <- map_dbl(spots, \(x) position_success(x))

results <- tibble(order_spot = spots, prob_view = chance_by_spot)

# Let's plot the results so we can better see the results of the simulation. I am using pink as the color as I like pink!
ggplot(results, aes(x = order_spot, y = prob_view)) +
  geom_line(color = "deeppink", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "deeppink", size = 0.8) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  labs(
    title = "Housing Lottery Simulation",
    subtitle = "Chance of getting a room with a beautiful view by lottery order",
    x = "Lottery order (1 = earliest pick)",
    y = "Probability of getting a room with a beautiful view"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








From the simulation I ran, we can see that the probability of receiving a room with a sea view remains roughly in this imaginary college remains constant across all lottery positions. This occurs because both the lottery order and the room assignments are randomized, meaning each student has approximately the same chance (around 40%) of getting a sea-view room. The fluctuations in the line represent random variation between simulation runs rather than systematic differences in opportunity.
